metadata.title: Claude, Gaps.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: did Claude learn to judge compliance risk when it picked up the gaps skill? Takes the skill apart, explains the machinery, and judges the design trade-off — a skill is a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, not new judgment.

beats.narration_text: People hear 'gaps skill' and assume Claude learned to weigh compliance risk. Wrong branch. Nothing in the model changed — it was handed a file to follow. So what's actually inside it?

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has a gaps skill' and it sounds like the model itself picked up compliance judgment — as if training added new legal-reasoning weight, and Claude now decides, on its own, what counts as a compliance gap. That's the natural read. It's also the wrong one.

Here's the test that gives it away. Delete the skill's folder, and Claude's compliance judgment sits exactly where it did — because it was never in the weights to begin with. All you removed was one routine it used to follow. Skills are external instructions, not internalized capability.

production_viz.label: NOTHING TO LOSE
production_viz.caption: there was no judgment to lose

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is, machinery down: one file. Gaps is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain steps for opening a tracker, reporting what's flagged and not yet closed, and updating an item when you close it or mark it risk-accepted. Claude reads that file before it starts. That's the whole apparatus.

The execution model is dead simple: read the file top to bottom, then do what it says, one step at a time, in the order written. No hidden control flow. Branches exist only where the file itself writes 'if this, then that.'

So a skill is a specification, not a new power. That trade-off cuts two ways. The payoff: the same tracker check every run — what's open, what's closed, what's been risk-accepted — because Claude is following the same file each time. The cost: anything the file didn't anticipate is off the map.

So gaps never taught Claude how to judge a compliance risk — and it never had to. What it guarantees is consistency: every run reads the same file, follows the same steps, reports the tracker the same way. That's the whole trick. That's what you're actually buying.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN
production_viz.caption: same file, same report, every run

beats.narration_text: This has a sharp consequence in both directions. A clean close isn't proof of understanding — the file can be followed to the letter on a case Claude never really evaluated. A mishandled update isn't proof of a broken skill — it may just be a case the file's steps don't cover. What you're evaluating is the fit between the routine and the situation, not Claude's grasp of the risk.
A skill doesn't teach Claude how to judge compliance risk — it's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so every tracker check comes out the same way, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one status check I run the same way every time. Write me a SKILL.md for it — plain language, ordered steps — then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll do, before you do it. Go deeper: hand the same model a status check with one recurring exception it never quite fits, and ask it where the steps would silently start filling in judgment you never wrote down — because that's the seam where a skill quietly goes off the map.
